UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Increasing Market and Planning Efficiency                             Docket No: AD10-12-17
Through improved Software


                            Post-technical Conference Comments of Greg Poulos

    I.   Introduction and Issue Summary
On July 7, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) convened a
technical conference on transmission planning and cost management. On July 20, 2026, the
Commission issued a notice inviting post-technical conference written comments. These
comments respond to the Commission’s notice inviting written comments and are offered in
addition to the oral comments I provided to the Commission during the technical conference.

Again, I would like to thank the Commission for tackling this very important area of concern for
consumers. I note that I am again acting on my own behalf and not representing the interests of
the Consumer Advocates of the PJM States (CAPS)1 or the state appointed consumer advocate
members of CAPS as part of the views I share in this document.

You cannot address what you cannot measure. Long-term load forecasting plays an integral part
in determining the capacity that must be procured, the transmission lines that must be built, and
ultimately the price customers must pay for electricity in the region. While progress has been
made, consumer confidence in PJM’s long-term forecasting remains low. The clock is ticking,
the unprecedented expansion of data center load and its projected accelerating trend into the future
becomes a bigger concern by the day. The adverse consequences of inaccurate load forecasting,
not grounded in use of the best forecasting methodologies, are greater and greater.

Important public policy principles have been established to enable data center deployment but also
to protect ordinary households from bearing the costs of the grid expansion needed to connect data
centers and, instead, map responsibility for those costs to the data centers driving the grid
expansion.2 Improvements in load forecasting, particularly of large load/data centers, are a
necessary effort to better achieve these principles.

1
  I have been the Executive Director of CAPS since April, 2017. Established in 2013, CAPS is a nonprofit
organization whose members include state consumer advocate offices in 13 PJM states and the District of Columbia.
As a whole, the CAPS members represent over 65-million consumers throughout the PJM footprint. As the
Executive Director of CAPS, I coordinate the efforts of the sixteen member offices, stay active in the PJM
stakeholder process, and monitor relevant proceedings at the Commission to ensure that the prices consumers pay
for reliable, wholesale electric service are reasonable.

                                                        1
 In these written comments, I want to supplement the record by identifying specific areas of concern
raised by my colleagues in the consumer advocate offices directly to PJM regarding PJM’s conduct
of load forecasting:3

      •   PJM must apply best practices for its large load forecasting. There is a developing body of
          expert, regulatory and industry commentary that describe these practices and PJM should
          seek to incorporate them.

      •   PJM needs to adopt robust, mandatory, minimum uniform financial/contractual
          commitment requirements applicable to all large loads.

      •   PJM should incorporate review and analysis of the existing experience with data center
          large loads.

      •   PJM forecasting practice should incorporate pending policy developments that will affect
          large loads.

    II.   Comments
The explosive predictions of data center load for our region brings a pressing need for major
enhancements in data center electric load forecasting. As presented in the graphic below, if PJM’s
2024 forecast is to be believed, we can expect approximately 52 GW of new data center electricity
load in the PJM region by 2032.4 This is the equivalent of the entire California ISO load5 moving
to the PJM region over the next 5 years. Moreover, large load/data center load is the overwhelming
contributor to projected massive load growth in PJM for the next decade at least.




developers, and cooperatives, and state governors, including the governors of PJM states Tennessee, West Virginia,
Ohio, and Indiana.”
3

                                                        2
 Striving for greater accuracy in load forecasting has huge reliability and financial consequences
for electric consumers. For example, the load growth projected in PJM’s annually produced
forecasts drive billions in electric transmission investment and generation cost because of its use
in PJM’s transmission planning and the administration of its capacity market.

PJM has made a number of reforms to the Large Load Analysis process in an effort to address the
challenge to its forecasting practices posed by data centers. As noted below, consumer advocates
have presented PJM with specific areas that need further reform to better address the growing
challenge.

1. Adoption of Best Practices for large load (data center load) forecasting.

While PJM has been working to develop improvements in its large load forecasting protocols,
several expert and industry- based efforts have progressed to identify best practices for forecasting
of large loads, particularly data centers. Reports produced by these efforts are now available.6 PJM
should endeavor to incorporate these best practices into its procedures to the maximum extent
possible. Some of the advocate offices are concerned that PJM’s proposed protocol reforms
seemingly do not incorporate or reflect these recent developments.

 2. Mandatory robust minimum, uniform financial and contractual requirements for
individual large loads are needed.

Relying upon its legacy practices, PJM’s protocol for review of large loads continues to rely
predominantly on submissions from individual Transmission Owners and load serving entities

6
 See, e.g., ESIG Large Loads Task Force (ESIG LLTF), Forecasting for Large Loads: Current Practices and
Recommendations (December, 2025); ESIG LLTF, Large Load Performance Requirements: Current Practices and
Recommendations (January, 2026); North American Electric Reliability Council, Assessment of Gaps in Existing
Practices, Requirements and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads (March, 2026);

                                                      3
 which may, and will, vary based on the entity submitting the information. Simply put, the level
and quality of information provided and analysis conducted in developing PJM’s load forecast
needs to improve.

PJM’s large load protocol reform requires increased disclosure of information developed and
submitted by the Transmission Owners and load serving entities. However, from our perspective,
it still does not give PJM the full ability to verify the large load information that will be
incorporated into PJM’s analysis. The Transmission Owners, load service entities and the data
centers must be required to meet robust and uniform minimum requirements regarding the
information required.

Assuring robust and uniform requirements for financial commitment from data centers, and its
incorporation into PJM’s load forecasting practices is critical. It forces data centers to have “skin
in the game” and provides price signals better aligned with cost causation. Both these factors assist
in weeding out duplicative and speculative customer service requests, otherwise exacerbating the
load forecasting challenge. Moreover, adherence to uniform robust standards across the
Transmission Owners mitigate incentives for service territory shopping in a race to the bottom.

Some of the consumer advocate offices I am working with are concerned that the reliance on
existing Transmission Owner requirements for data center contractual/financial commitments is a
material weak spot in PJM’s load forecasting. This position is supported by the NERC March
2026 Large Loads Working Group White Paper.7 The NERC White Paper addresses “gaps” in
utility activities relating to the forecasting of large loads, representing deficiencies in current
practice.

        Demand forecasts are developed by utilities, system planners, and PCs [Planning
        Coordinators]. The PCs may source some or all of their demand forecasts from
        member utilities and may also develop portions of the demand forecast themselves.
        In the case of information on large loads, PCs, TPs [Transmission Planners], and
        RPs [Resource Planners] are mostly or wholly dependent on information provided
        by the utilities, which may lead to forecasts relying on what has become out-of-date
        information.

        Some system planners provide guidance to their members on the information that
        they require and collaborate with their members on practices. Some utilities and
        system planners have established standardized practices (e.g., via gates, stages,
        policy support, financial commitment) for evaluating the key forecasting
        parameters as large loads request interconnection and engage in obtaining utility
        service or otherwise securing power. The divergence of large load demand forecasts
        is a result of the lack of well-established practices…8

7
  North American Electric Reliability Corporation, Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and
Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads (NERC Large Loads Working Group White Paper) March 2026.
8
  North American Electric Reliability Corporation, Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and
Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads, (NERC Large Loads Working Group White Paper) March 2026 at

                                                      4
 PJM does provide some guidance to the Transmission Owners and load serving entities.9 The
practices followed by the individual Transmission Owners submitting large load information are
not standardized and thus, lack the assurance around the adequate levels of financial and
contractual commitments that should be expected from data center loads.

3. Incorporation of historical experience with data center loads.

While it still may be early in the data center growth phase, experience is accruing with data center
loads and that experience should be rigorously reviewed and analyzed. In turn, that analysis should
inform PJM’s annual load forecasting cycles.

To date, PJM has addressed data center loads exclusively through the large load analysis process.
The data has been based on individual Transmission Owner reporting of data center customer
service requests. PJM’s analysis of data center load does not appear to be as robust as the approach
relied upon for other broadly defined customer groupings. For example, forecasts for other
customer groups are rolled up into the RTO-level and zonal forecasts. In addition, the forecasts of
other customer groups are primarily based on an econometric analysis led by PJM of prior
consumption patterns in relation to correlated economic variables and weather variations.

Furthermore, PJM’s review should also include analysis of experienced data center project
capacity utilization and ramping rates, data center differentiation (among collocated data centers,
hyperscalers and other broad data center customer types) and project triage/cancellations (and the
circumstances of the cancellations and their comparison to prior projections).

Finally, we would like to see the review include probabilistically developed scenarios that include
the possibility of recessions, supply chain constraints and technology. In turn, the Transmission
Owners and load serving entities should be required to provide this information to the extent
available to them on a systematic basis to PJM.

PJM has announced it will do an annual formal true-up each May of prior periods of data center
load growth. The devil will be in the details. The consumer advocates have asked for the true-up
to include information such as: project triage, project ramping, project utilization and project delay
for the prior period under review. The review should also include an analysis of probabilities of
recession, financial and credit risks, impact of other economy wide variables on data center growth,
feasible pacing of large load grid interconnections, supply chain limitations and other matters. PJM
recently did issue such an assessment for its last annual forecast cycle.10 While an improvement
over prior practice, that review still did not address many of the items of analysis which consumer
advocates had requested of PJM and which are a necessary practice in continuous improvement.




9
    See, PJM, Manual 19: Load Forecasting and Analysis, Attachment B (Load Forecast Adjustment Guidelines).
10
     PJM Resource Adequacy Planning Department, 2026 PJM Load Forecast Accuracy Report (May 29, 2026).

                                                        5
 4. PJM Must integrate parallel reforms made to PJM’s capacity market and transmission
planning practices as well as developing state-level large load retail tariffs.

The Data Center electricity load is projected to arrive in a very short period and in very large
quantity. Consumer advocates representatives have asked PJM to ensure it can timely adjust to
the landscape. For example, PJM needs to ensure it can incorporate material adjustments during
the contemporaneous annual load forecasting cycle. In addition, PJM has a number of market and
planning developments currently under consideration that will, or likely will, affect data center
large loads and their trajectory over the forecast period.

PJM needs timely projections that include:

1. Data center adoption of firm and/or non-firm contract demand transmission arrangements
coupled with collocated behind-the-meter generation.

2. Data center adoption of load curtailment measures.

3. Data center adoption of “bring your own new generation” (BYONG) projects to match their
projected loads (plus a proportionate reserve margin, as advocated under several proposals
currently under consideration in a PJM stakeholder process).

4. Data center adherence to applicable state-level large load retail tariffs (which may require
BYONG, adherence to early curtailment and/or demand response measures, among other matters).

III.   Conclusion

I conclude by expressing my sincere gratitude to the Commission for providing consumers with
the opportunity to be heard on such a vital issue.


Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Gregory J. Poulos

Gregory J. Poulos

August 19, 2026
